name: Ibaraki-dōji
description: Ibaraki-dōji is a celebrated oni (demon) of Heian-period Japanese legend, the chief retainer of the demon king Shuten-dōji and the antagonist of the famous Rashōmon / Modori-bashi episode in which the warrior Watanabe no Tsuna severs its arm.
full_description: Ibaraki-dōji (茨木童子) is one of the most famous oni in Japanese folklore, traditionally the chief lieutenant of the great oni-king Shuten-dōji of Mount Ōe. Two main birth-origin traditions place the demon either at Sunagodzuka in Echigo (modern Niigata) or in Settsu (modern Osaka / Hyōgo). The character's gender is ambiguous in the source tradition, sometimes a male oni and sometimes a kijo (female oni). The most famous narrative is set in late Heian Kyoto: Watanabe no Tsuna, one of the Four Guardian Kings (Shitennō) of Minamoto no Yorimitsu (Raikō), encounters a beautiful young woman who reveals herself as Ibaraki-dōji and attempts to abduct him, either at the Modori-bashi bridge over the Ichijō or at the Rashōmon gate. Tsuna severs the demon's arm with his sword Higekiri (also called Onikiri / Onikirimaru). Warned by an onmyōji (often Abe no Seimei) to confine himself for seven days, Tsuna is on the seventh night tricked by Ibaraki-dōji, who appears disguised as his aunt and reclaims the arm. The episode is a foundational story-cycle of the demon-slaying repertoire and is told across the Konjaku monogatari, the Tsurugi-no-maki of the Heike monogatari, the Genpei jōsuiki, the Taiheiki, the Settsuyō gundan (1701), and a long line of nō, kabuki and ukiyo-e treatments.
origin: The Ibaraki-dōji legend is centered on Heian-period Kyoto and on the surrounding regions of Settsu (modern Osaka, Hyōgo) and Echigo (modern Niigata).

etymology.origin: Ibaraki-dōji combines the place-name Ibaraki — variously read as Ibaraki in Settsu (modern Osaka) or as the Ibaraki of Echigo — with dōji (童子, 'child'), a term used for oni offspring and for young oni-attendants rather than for biological children.
etymology.first_use: Medieval otogi-zōshi and gunki-monogatari (Heike monogatari Tsurugi-no-maki, Genpei jōsuiki, Taiheiki) of the 13th–14th centuries; the Settsuyō gundan (1701) consolidates the Settsu tradition.

timeline.event: Compilation of Konjaku monogatari (early 12th century) and Heike monogatari Tsurugi-no-maki (13th century), containing early forms of the Watanabe no Tsuna / Ibaraki-dōji episode
timeline.significance: Earliest attestations of the legend in Japanese literature

timeline.event: Composition of the nō play Rashōmon (attributed to Kanze school, 15th century)
timeline.significance: Early dramatic treatment of the Rashōmon variant

timeline.event: Settsuyō gundan published, consolidating the Settsu version of Ibaraki-dōji's birth narrative
timeline.significance: Major Edo-period source for the Settsu tradition

timeline.event: Kabuki play Ibaraki (茨木) premieres, written for Onoe Kikugorō V
timeline.significance: Foundational kabuki dramatization of the post-encounter retrieval scene; remains a canonical role

timeline.event: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi includes 'Old Woman Taking Away the Oni's Arm' (Rōba ki wo motte saru no zu) in Shinkei Sanjūrokkaisen, completed 1892
timeline.significance: Most-reproduced visual treatment of the Ibaraki-dōji legend in modern times

related.name: Shuten-dōji
related.description: The oni-king of Mount Ōe whom Ibaraki-dōji serves as chief lieutenant

related.name: Oni
related.description: The general class of Japanese demonic ogres to which Ibaraki-dōji belongs

related.name: Kijo
related.description: Female oni; some traditions class Ibaraki-dōji as kijo

cultural_notes: Severed oni arms must be guarded with ritual seclusion (the seven-day kessai) overseen by an onmyōji; oni can shapeshift into human form, especially as elderly female relatives, and so social trust itself becomes a site of demonic ambush.

sources.title: Shinkei Sanjūrokkaisen (Thirty-Six New Forms of Ghosts)
